one_liner: From-scratch Hopper BF16 GEMM (TMA + WGMMA) beating cuBLAS by 2-7% on square H100 matmuls, plus a CUB-level reduction.
what_it_does: A small collection of hand-written CUDA kernels: twelve progressively optimized H100 BF16 matrix-multiply kernels (h100/matmul/matmul_1..12.cuh) driven by one benchmark binary that also runs cuBLAS as kernel 0, four int32 sum-reduction kernels compared with cub::DeviceReduce::Sum, and a ten-rung NVFP4 GEMM ladder for GB300 compared with cuBLASLt. Each matmul kernel is exposed as a host function runKernelN(M, N, K, A, B, C, DB) taking device pointers: A is row-major M x K, B is stored N x K (K-contiguous), C is written in BF16 in the column-major layout the cuBLAS reference uses. It is example code, not a library API: no streams, alpha/beta, batching or shape dispatch.
how_it_is_fast: The final kernels (11/12) are persistent, warp-specialized Hopper GEMMs: one producer warpgroup issues TMA bulk-tensor loads (cp.async.bulk.tensor with 128B swizzle, multicast across a 2-CTA thread-block cluster) into a 3-stage mbarrier-synchronized shared-memory ring, while two consumer warpgroups run wgmma.mma_async m64n256k16 BF16 instructions with FP32 accumulators, and setmaxnreg moves registers from producer to consumers. Output tiles (128 x 256, BK=64) are assigned to 128 persistent CTAs along a Hilbert curve for L2 reuse, and kernel 12 writes C through stmatrix into padded shared memory followed by a TMA store. The sum kernels use int4 vector loads (16 per thread), redux.sync warp reductions, one shared-memory atomic per warp and one global atomicAdd per block.
when_to_use: Large square or near-square BF16 GEMMs (the published sizes are 4096 and 8192) on an H100 SXM, with M and N multiples of 256 and K a multiple of 64.

Learning or prototyping Hopper GEMM design: the 12-kernel ladder goes from a naive kernel to TMA, WGMMA, warp specialization, clusters and Hilbert scheduling in plain CUDA plus inline PTX, without CUTLASS/CuTe templates.
A starting point for a custom fused epilogue on Hopper when you control shapes and want a single-file kernel you can edit.
Studying Blackwell (GB300/B300, sm_103a) NVFP4 GEMM: the gb300/nvfp4 ladder documents each optimization rung and a paired, cooldown-gated benchmark protocol against cuBLASLt.
when_not_to_use: Arbitrary shapes: nothing checks divisibility at runtime (the Makefile's -DNDEBUG compiles out every assert), and issue #4 (open) reports row-shuffled wrong results from matmul_3 at 128x128x64 on an H800.
Any GPU other than an H100-class sm_90a part: kernels are compiled only for sm_90a, NUM_SM is hard-coded to 128 persistent CTAs, and nothing is tuned for H100 PCIe/H800/H200.

When a 2-7% gain does not justify owning a kernel: the margin is about 1.07x at N=4096 and 1.02x at N=8192 (derived from page data), and issue #13 (open, 'Unable to reproduce reported numbers') reports much lower absolute throughput on another H100 (cuBLAS 518.6 TFLOPS at N=8192).
FP16, FP8, transposed, batched or alpha/beta GEMMs, or multi-threaded host code: none are supported, and runKernelN keeps TMA descriptors and the schedule buffer in host globals.
General reductions: the sum kernels handle int32 only, require N divisible by 4, and win by about 1.5% over CUB.

integration.dependencies: CUDA toolkit with the Driver API (cuTensorMapEncodeTiled, -lcuda); cuBLAS only for the reference/verification path; CUB for the sum comparison
integration.min_toolchain: C++17 nvcc with sm_90a support (Makefile: -gencode arch=compute_90a,code=sm_90a); CUDA 12.6 named only in a search snippet of the worklog, and issue #13 built it with CUDA 12.4; the GB300 NVFP4 kernels need CUDA 13.1 and sm_103a
integration.platforms: NVIDIA H100 (sm_90a) for matmul and sum; GB300/B300 (sm_103a) for gb300/nvfp4; Linux build via GNU Make
integration.thread_safety: not documented; runKernel11/12 cache TMA descriptors and the Hilbert schedule in host-global variables, so concurrent calls with different shapes are unsafe
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: false - fixed-layout runKernelN(M, N, K, A, B, C) host functions with no handle, stream, alpha/beta or transpose arguments; not a cublasGemmEx replacement

gotchas: Kernel 12 needs M and N multiples of 256 (BM 128 x 2-CTA cluster, BN 256) and K a multiple of 64 (num_blocks_k = K / BK drops any tail); with -DNDEBUG the device and host asserts that guard this are compiled out, so bad shapes fail silently.

runKernel11/12 rebuild their cached TMA maps only when M changes (keyed on _prev_m), so calling with the same M but a different N or K reuses stale descriptors; each rebuild also cudaMallocs a new schedule buffer without freeing the old one.

The matmul harness hard-codes 8192 x 8192 (max_size), times 8 back-to-back launches after one verification run, uses a 0.1 absolute tolerance on BF16 outputs, and keeps benchmarking after a failed check; reproducing the N=4096 row means editing the source.

The sum kernels zero *d_out from inside the kernel (thread i == 0) while other blocks atomicAdd to it, a formal race; the benchmark's own int32 total (2^30 values of rand() % 100, about 5.3e10, derived) wraps, identically in CUB.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over ThunderKittens when you want one readable, dependency-free Hopper GEMM file to fork rather than a tile-abstraction framework that matches cuBLAS more generally; pick it over bare-metal when the target is an H100 instead of an sm_86 laptop GPU, where bare-metal's margin is about 1.02x under a clock lock. For quantized or GEMV work, BitBLAS or FastGEMV fit better.
verified_claims_summary: On one H100 (SXM 80GB and CUDA 12.6 per a worklog search snippet), the same binary timed the custom BF16 GEMM against cublasGemmEx (BF16 in and out, CUBLAS_COMPUTE_32F, CUBLAS_GEMM_DEFAULT): 763 vs 716 TFLOPS at N=4096 and 808 vs 795 at N=8192 (about 1.07x and 1.02x, derived from page data); the README does not say which of kernels 1-12 produced them. An independent run in issue #13 (H100 variant unstated, CUDA 12.4, N=8192) measured cuBLAS at 518.6 TFLOPS and kernels 10/12 at 533.4/530.8 TFLOPS, about 1.02-1.03x (derived from page data), so the small margin held there though absolute numbers were far lower. The int32 sum of 2^30 elements ran at 3240.11 GB/s vs CUB's 3193.36 GB/s.
status_note: Active (last commit 2026-08-15, 625 stars, MIT, 17 commits) and small enough to vendor, but it is a demonstration repo: open issues #4 (small-shape wrong results) and #13 (reproducibility) have no maintainer replies.
